hook: Warren Sturgis McCulloch was born on November 16, 1898, in Orange, New Jersey, and trained in medicine, earning his M.D. from Columbia University in 1927 after an undergraduate degree at Yale. He worked as a neurologist and psychiatrist at institutions including Bellevue Hospital and Rockland State Hospital before turning to research on the organization of the nervous system, joining the University of Illinois as a professor of psychiatry in 1941. There he met the young, largely self-taught logician Walter Pitts, and together in 1943 they published A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity, modeling networks of neurons as logical, all-or-none units capable of computing propositions in Boolean logic. McCulloch moved to MIT's Research Laboratory of Electronics in 1952, where he continued studying probabilistic models of brain function and helped organize the Macy Conferences that founded the field of cybernetics, serving as the first president of the American Society for Cybernetics in 1967. He died of an apparent heart seizure on September 24, 1969, at his home near Old Lyme, Connecticut.

quick_facts: Born November 16, 1898, in Orange, New Jersey, and died September 24, 1969, near Old Lyme, Connecticut.
Earned his M.D. from Columbia University in 1927 after undergraduate study at Yale.
Became professor of psychiatry at the University of Illinois in 1941, where he began working with Walter Pitts.
Co-authored A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity with Pitts in 1943.
Joined MIT's Research Laboratory of Electronics in 1952.
Served as the first president of the American Society for Cybernetics starting in 1967.

achievements.title: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity (1943)
achievements.impact: Created the first mathematical model treating neurons as logical units, a foundation later cited by researchers building artificial neural networks.

achievements.title: Organizing role in the Macy Conferences on cybernetics
achievements.impact: Helped bring together researchers from neuroscience, mathematics and engineering whose exchanges founded cybernetics as a field connecting biological and artificial information processing.

achievements.title: Embodiments of Mind (1965)
achievements.impact: Collected decades of his papers on the physical basis of thought, influencing later research at the intersection of neuroscience and computing.
